title: The Mystery of Steubenville
author: Tim Daly
summary: Tim Daly investigates Steubenville, Ohio, an Appalachian steel town district that Emily Hanford's Sold a Story podcast surfaced as an academic outlier, using Stanford's Education Opportunity Project's grade-level-unit metric to show its students perform more than two grade levels above the national average across virtually every subgroup, including a Black-student average that exceeds the overall national average, something none of the ten largest US districts achieves. He deliberately compares Steubenville to systems most likely to explain away its results and finds each explanation fails: it spends less per pupil than similar districts, its teacher credentials and staffing levels are unremarkable, and a direct comparison to wealthy Beverly Hills shows Steubenville's low-income students outscoring even Beverly Hills's non-poor students despite a roughly $18,000 per-pupil spending gap. What does hold up is a cluster of unglamorous execution factors: chronic student absenteeism roughly a third of the state average, teachers themselves attending school at rates well above comparable urban districts, and a decades-long, faithfully implemented commitment to the Success for All model despite thousands of other schools using the same program without similar results. Daly's conclusion is that Steubenville's real differentiator isn't a secret curriculum but sustained, minutely aligned daily execution across every classroom, arguing that turning ordinary execution into an institutional way of life, not selecting the right program, is what actually built the district's decade-long dynasty.
points: Uses Stanford's Education Opportunity Project grade-level-unit metric to make Steubenville's outlier status numerically precise: plus 2.33 grade levels above the national average, with even its Black-student subgroup average exceeding the overall national average, a result none of the ten largest US districts achieves.

Constructs a direct, resource-controlled comparison to wealthy Beverly Hills (nearly $30,000 vs. under $12,000 per pupil) showing Steubenville's low-income students outscore even Beverly Hills's non-poor students, systematically ruling out spending as the explanatory variable.

Methodically eliminates the most common alternative explanations one at a time - superintendent charisma, demographics, funding, teacher credentials, teaching to the test - before naming what actually differs, modeling a rigorous process of elimination rather than asserting a single cause.

Quantifies attendance as a specific, measurable mechanism: students attending roughly 96 additional days across a K-12 career (over half a year of extra schooling) and teachers present 96.1% of days versus far higher absenteeism in comparable Ohio cities.

Distinguishes program selection from program execution by noting thousands of schools have used the same Success for All model without Steubenville's results, concluding the real differentiator is faithful, minutely aligned daily execution sustained over a decade, not which off-the-shelf curriculum was chosen.
quotes: Steubenville's performance for reading and math is plus 2.33, meaning its students in grades 3-8 are more than two grade levels above the national average.
None of the ten largest districts in the EOP data set has Black student performance equal to the national average, let alone exceeding it.
Poor students in Steubenville have higher scores than non-poor students in Beverly Hills.

Most American districts peaked in performance between 2013 and 2015 before entering a prolonged decline. As of 2025, Steubenville students were achieving at higher rates in both math and reading than they were a decade ago.
In 2024-25, just 7.2 percent of Steubenville students were chronically absent, versus 25 percent statewide. For Black students specifically, 9.3 percent versus 43 percent for the rest of Ohio.
Teachers in Steubenville attended 96.1 percent of days in 2024-25. Teachers in Cleveland, Columbus, and Toledo were absent more than twice as often.
Thousands of schools have used SFA over the years, and most have not become anything like Steubenville. Steubenville did not possess some preternatural judgment to select a magic bean program.

Teachers across schools were generally teaching the same material, with the same methods, at the same time. Which is the hardest trick in education. Turn everyday execution into a way of life. That's how you build a dynasty.
